To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a model of radiation induced bystander cell kill may be applied to radiotherapy treatment planning and may influence the degree of dose heterogenity within a target volume.

1) the bystander effect may be important in the context of radiotherapy treatment planning, 2) the bystander model predicts a degree of dose heterogenity that is as good or better than uniform dose in terms EUD and TCP, 3) the bystander and standard LQ models differ by 2-3 Gy at a dose of 78 Gy.
The results suggest the bystander model may allow for some degree of dose inhomogeneity within a prostate CTV, although the results are highly sensitive to the assumptions of the model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of bystander cell killing on the outcome of radiotherapy treatment planning for prostate cancer.
understanding the potential for dose heterogeneity within target volumes to influence tumour control probability and equivalent uniform dose.
investigating whether the bystander effect influences cell kill within a prostate target volume.

the bystander model is an interesting and potentially important concept that may be applicable in a clinical setting and warrants further investigation.
this work demonstrates that the potential for a bystander effect in radiotherapy warrants further study, particularly with regard to the potential for dose heterogeneity to influence TCP.
the results suggest the potential of a bystander model to deviate from common local LQ models as dose heterogeneity is varied, although the results are based on broad and simplifying assumptions.

the bystander effect may influence the treatment plan for intermediate risk prostate cancer patients.
